new_statements.quote: Phonetically long, heavily stressed vowels are in phonemic contrast with vowels which are short and weakly stressed. The analysis has not proceeded far enough for a phonemic interpretation of this contrast to be formulated solely in terms of short versus long, or stressed versus unstressed vowels. In the following examples vowel length is marked [:] and heavy stress [´]. [quru] "spear fish," [qú:ru] "pound nuts;" [tulu] "mute," [tú:lu] "three;" [mana] "past tense," [má:na] "blessing," [ká:kiti] "bite," [ká:kí:ti] "open up a boil;" [beré:] "how about you?", [bé:re] "laugh;" [kula] "dance," [kú:la] "elephantiasis."
new_statements.citation: Whaley, Owen G. 1962. Babatana segmental phonemes. Te Reo 5: 60-62.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (3 pp., CamScanner image PDF, no text layer; extracted text returns only form feeds) and rendered page 1 (= Te Reo 5 p. 60; page 2 carries the printed number '61.') to a PNG in the Section 1.3 'Stress and Vowel Length' is on page 1 and the quoted passage is there verbatim, including all six pairs [quru]/[qú:ru], [tulu]/[tú:lu], [mana]/[má:na], [ká:kiti]/[ká:kí:ti], [beré:]/[bé:re], [kula]/[kú:la]; the held. mangles the acute accents ([ta:lul, [ki:lal etc.) but the report's quote follows the page image, not the scanned. The section says only that long/heavily-stressed vowels contrast phonemically with short/weakly-stressed ones and that 'the analysis has not proceeded far enough' to d…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand statement on Babatana proper says that a heavy-stress-plus-length prominence is phonemically contrastive (minimal pairs where one member has a long, heavily stressed vowel and the other none, plus one positional pair beré: vs bé:re), but the author explicitly leaves open whether the contrast is one of length or of stress; no rule for the position of stress is given. Laycock 1982: 274 doubts the contrast and suggests it may follow from stress and/or open vs closed (underlyingly consonant-final) syllables. The nearest modern description, Ross 2002 on the sister variety Sisiqa (sisi1250), gives a penultimate default with secondary stress on the pre-antepenult and antepenult stress in echo-vowel words, which is what Laycock's suspicion would predict for Babatana; if that transfers, Babatana would read fixed-penult on underlying forms, but no source states this for Babatana itself.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Whaley 1962. Ross 2002: 457 (Sisiqa, not Babatana) gives secondary stress on the pre-antepenult if any.
new_statements.exceptions: Whaley: none stated beyond the contrast itself. Ross 2002 (Sisiqa): reduplicated monosyllables take final stress (/zo'zo/ walk, /mi'mi/ see); certain tri- and tetrasyllables with identical last two vowels take antepenult stress (/'okene/ moon, /'ləgoto/ root, /mə'ləkana/ sky, /bə'lukuru/ wing), analysed as underlyingly consonant-final echo-vowel words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated citation forms elicited from one speaker (Esau Tuza) in phonetic transcription; Whaley defines the word as the 'minimal isolable utterance part'. Orthography does not mark the contrast (p. 62).
new_statements.identity_note: Whaley 1962 describes Babatana proper (informant Esau Tuza, Choiseul) = baba1268. The best modern description in the area, Ross 2002 'Sisiqa' (The Oceanic Languages 456-466, saved here), describes Sisiqa/Seqa (Senga, Sengga), which Glottolog codes as a separate language sisi1250, sister of baba1268 under East Choiseul (east2760); Tryon & Hackman 1983 and Ethnologue/Wikipedia treat it as a dialect of East Choiseul/Babatana, and Ross says its speakers are bilingual in Babatana with the differences eroding. For sisi1250 Ross 2002: 457 reads fixed-penult (secondary on the pre-antepenult; final stress in reduplicated monosyllables; antepenult in echo-vowel words) — this is the statement the sisi1250 target (scan verdict SOURCE-NAMED-UNREACHABLE) was missing.

sources.citation: Whaley, Owen G. 1962. Babatana segmental phonemes. Te Reo 5: 60-62.
sources.quote: Phonetically long, heavily stressed vowels are in phonemic contrast with vowels which are short and weakly stressed. The analysis has not proceeded far enough for a phonemic interpretation of this contrast to be formulated solely in terms of short versus long, or stressed versus unstressed vowels. In the following examples vowel length is marked [:] and heavy stress [´]. [quru] "spear fish," [qú:ru] "pound nuts;" [tulu] "mute," [tú:lu] "three;" [mana] "past tense," [má:na] "blessing," [ká:kiti] "bite," [ká:kí:ti] "open up a boil;" [beré:] "how about you?", [bé:re] "laugh;" [kula] "dance," [kú:la] "elephantiasis."
sources.note: Sec. 1.3 'Stress and Vowel Length' (p. 60): long, heavily stressed vowels are in phonemic contrast with short, weakly stressed ones; author states the analysis has not gone far enough to decide whether the contrast is length or stress; six minimal pairs given ([quru]/[qú:ru], [tulu]/[tú:lu], [mana]/[má:na], [ká:kiti]/[ká:kí:ti], [beré:]/[bé:re], [kula]/[kú:la]); orthography does not mark it (p. 62). No positional rule. Babatana proper, informant Esau Tuza.

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm. 2002. Sisiqa. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds), The Oceanic Languages, 456-466. Richmond: Curzon.
sources.note: SISIQA, not Babatana proper (Glottolog sisi1250, sister language under East Choiseul; Tryon & Hackman 1983 treat it as a dialect of East Choiseul). Sec. 1.2 'Phonotactics and stress', p. 457: 'Polysyllables are generally stressed on the penult, with secondary stress on the pre-antepenult if any. However, there are two exceptions to this pattern. Where a monosyllable is reduplicated, stress falls on the final syllable: /zo'zo/ walk... sources.citation: Tryon, D.T. & B.D. Hackman. 1983. Solomon Islands languages: an internal classification. Pacific Linguistics C-72. Canberra: ANU. 490 pp.
sources.note: Mbambatana listed as 'Central-East Choiseul' with Katazi, Sengga, Avaso, Lomaumbi etc. Sound-correspondence tables only; the word 'unstressed' appears just in reflex footnotes; no stress rule for any language.

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. 1982. Metathesis in Austronesian: Ririo and other cases. In A. Halim, L. Carrington & S.A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 1: Currents in Oceanic, 269-281. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
sources.note: Fieldwork Susuka 1978 with Babatana comparison lists. p. 274: 'Whaley also claims contrastive vowel length for Babatana, but I am not entirely sure that this is not a function of stress and/or open versus closed syllables.' p. 277: Ririo 'has essentially the same stress patterns as Babatana'. No rule for either language.
